summary: Tantalus (also called Atys) was a Lydian or Phrygian king, generally the son of Zeus and Pluto, and father of Pelops, Niobe, and Broteas. Famous for eternal torment in Tartarus — standing in a pool beneath fruit he can never reach, with water that always recedes — he is the namesake of "tantalise." Early Greek sources more often hang a threatening stone above his head; later tradition stresses the cannibal feast in which he served Pelops to the gods.
etymology: Ancient Greek Τάνταλος (Tántalos). Plato's Cratylus (395e) links the name to ταλάντατος, "who has to bear much," from τάλας, "wretched"; the Third Vatican Mythographer claimed it meant "wishing for a vision." Beekes rejected a secure Indo-European reading; Martin Litchfield West noted a possible echo of Hittite royal names such as Hantili.

sections.heading: Historical and geographic setting
paragraphs: Ancient writers place Tantalus in western Anatolia — Lydia around Mount Sipylus more often than inland Phrygia — sometimes calling him "King of Phrygia" even so. Pausanias knew a port and a conspicuous sepulcher associated with him; Strabo derived his wealth from Phrygian and Sipylan mines.

Near Mount Sipylus and Lake Karagöl ("Lake Tantalus") near ancient Smyrna, visitors were shown a tholos "tomb of Tantalus" and a rock-cut "throne of Pelops." References to "Pelops the Lydian" have led some scholars to treat the house as a primordial Lydian dynasty.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: He was generally son of Zeus and a woman named Pluto; a few sources give Tmolus as father. Wives are variously named — Dione daughter of Atlas, Euryanassa daughter of Pactolus, Clytia, or Eupryto. His children were Pelops, Niobe, and Broteas (a scholium adds Dascylus).

Through Pelops he was progenitor of the House of Atreus, whose misfortunes fill Greek tragedy. His grave-sanctuary stood on Sipylus, yet Argos claimed his bones and Lesbos kept a hero-shrine at Polion.

sections.heading: Punishment in Hades
paragraphs: The oldest surviving reference is Homer's Odyssey: Odysseus sees Tantalus in Hades, chin-deep in a pool beneath a fruit tree; wind blows the branches away, and the water recedes whenever he stoops to drink. Homer does not name the crime. An early fragment tradition (Nostoi, Archilochus, Alcman, Alcaeus, Pherecydes) instead hangs a giant rock above his head so that fear keeps him from enjoying a godlike banquet — the "Tantalean punishments" of Greek proverb.

Pausanias describes Polygnotus's painting in the Knidian Lesche at Delphi as combining both torments. Apollodorus likewise records the rock and the receding food and drink together. The English verb "tantalise" preserves the unreachable-desire image.

sections.heading: Crimes and the feast of Pelops
paragraphs: Surviving sources disagree on the offence. Pindar's Olympian 1 rejects the story that Tantalus butchered Pelops and served him to the gods — calling that a neighbour's slander after Poseidon carried the boy off — and instead charges Tantalus with stealing nectar and ambrosia to share with mortal friends. Other traditions accuse him of revealing divine secrets or of living too boldly like the gods.

The cannibal-banquet version, clearly familiar by Pindar's day and dominant in later reception, has the gods restore Pelops (Clotho or Rhea reviving him in a cauldron, with an ivory shoulder replacing the part Demeter had eaten in distraction). A separate Anatolian strand implicates Tantalus in the theft or false oath over Rhea's golden watchdog from Crete, for which Zeus blasts him and piles Sipylus upon him.

sections.heading: In drama and art
paragraphs: In Aeschylus's lost Niobe, Tantalus arrives at Thebes after Artemis and Apollo have slain Niobe's children, tries in vain to comfort his daughter, and escorts her home to Lydia. Seneca's Thyestes opens with Tantalus's ghost, driven by a Fury to sow enmity between his grandsons Atreus and Thyestes.

All known ancient depictions date from the fifth century BC onward. The Underworld Painter's Apulian volute-krater shows him fleeing the overhanging rock; the Velletri sarcophagus shows him scooping water that will not reach his lips.
